note: A man from the valley of Beit Hortan stuck four poles into the four corners of his field and stretched a vine across the top of them. According to the translation, he meant this to count as a wall around the field, so that he could plant near a vineyard without breaking the rule against mixing crops. The case came before the Sages, and they permitted it for the purpose of diverse kinds.
why: The Gemara wants to show that Rabbi Yohanan agrees with Rav that a doorway-shaped opening does not count as a wall if it is very wide. It cites this case, on which Reish Lakish says the field also counts as enclosed for Shabbat and Rabbi Yohanan says it does not.

terms.meaning: The Torah's ban on planting certain mixed crops together, including grain or vegetables too close to a vineyard. A proper wall between them removes the problem.
Two upright posts with a crosspiece on top. In Jewish law it can count as a wall with a doorway in it, closing off an area.

note: Rav Nahman taught publicly, in the name of Shmuel, that one or two travelers may enclose an area of two beit se'a, and three, who count as a caravan, may enclose six. He was asked whether he had abandoned the majority view of the Rabbis to follow the lone opinion of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Nahman then had a speaker stand beside him and announced: What I told you was my error. He restated the rule so that a caravan of three is given as much space as it needs.
why: The Mishna and a baraita record a dispute over how much space travelers may enclose with makeshift partitions for carrying on Shabbat. After the story the Gemara asks whether Rav Nahman's corrected ruling mixes the two opposing views, and why that is allowed.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who taught a ruling in public and then publicly retracted it as a mistake.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav Nahman's teacher, called here Rabbeinu Shmuel, in whose name he taught.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: An earlier Sage whose minority view Rav Nahman was accused of following.

terms.meaning: A unit of area, roughly the field needed to sow a se'a of grain; two beit se'a is the area of the Tabernacle courtyard, about 5,000 square cubits.
A group of three or more travelers, who are given a larger area in which they may carry on Shabbat.
A person who stood beside a Sage teaching in public and announced his words loudly to the audience.

note: Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata brought a basket of fruit to Rav Natan bar Oshaya on the eve of Shabbat. As he was leaving, Rav Natan let him go down one step and then told him, Stay here tonight. The next morning Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata got up early and went home.
why: Ulla has ruled that a traveler who set out and was persuaded to turn back still counts as having set out, which affects how far he may walk on Shabbat. The Gemara then asks which Sages' views Rav Natan was following when he let his guest start out before inviting him to stay.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata
people.about: A Sage who brought a basket of fruit to Rav Natan bar Oshaya before Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Natan bar Oshaya
people.about: The host, who let his guest set out and then asked him to stay the night.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat a person may walk only a set distance (2,000 cubits) beyond his place of residence. Someone who sets out toward a point at the edge of that limit can count it as his residence and go 2,000 more.

note: One of Rabbi Eliezer's students issued a legal ruling in his presence. Rabbi Eliezer told his wife, Imma Shalom, that he would be surprised if this student lived out the year, and he did not live out the year. She asked him whether he was a prophet. He said he was not a prophet or the son of a prophet, but he had received a tradition: anyone who issues a ruling in his teacher's presence is liable to death.
why: Rava has ruled that a student who rules in his teacher's presence is liable to death but one who rules elsewhere is not. The Gemara tests this against the story, since a later report says the student was three parasangs away, and concludes the ruling was given in the teacher's presence.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose student ruled in his presence; he predicted the student would die within the year.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's wife, who asked him if he was a prophet.

terms.meaning: Here, deserving death at the hands of Heaven, not a punishment carried out by a court.

note: On a Shabbat, the warm water prepared for a baby's circumcision spilled. Rava had water in his own courtyard, and he told people to move his belongings from his men's room to the inner women's room; he would sit there and give up his rights to his courtyard so the water could be brought over. Ravina challenged him with Shmuel's view that rights cannot be given up from one courtyard to another, and Rava said he followed Rabbi Yohanan. Ravina asked why, then, Rava did not stay put and have the neighbors give their rights back afterward, as Rav allowed. Rava said that on that point he followed Shmuel, and the two argued over whether Shmuel's two rulings rest on the same reason. The text does not say what was finally done.
why: The Gemara is telling several incidents of circumcision water spilled on Shabbat. This one turns on the dispute between Rav and Shmuel about giving up and returning rights in a courtyard, which the Gemara then examines directly.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who offered to give up the rights to his courtyard so the baby's water could be carried.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who challenged Rava's plan with Shmuel's rulings.

terms.meaning: When neighbors sharing a courtyard did not set up an eiruv, one may give up his share of the courtyard for Shabbat, so the others may carry there.
An arrangement, made before Shabbat, that turns several homes and a shared courtyard into one domain so that carrying between them is allowed.
The outer room of a house, opening onto the courtyard; the women's chamber was an inner room that did not.

note: A Sadducee lived in the same alleyway in Jerusalem as Rabban Gamliel and gave up his rights to the alleyway before Shabbat. Rabban Gamliel told his sons to hurry and take out and bring in whatever they needed before that loathsome man took out his own things and made the alleyway forbidden to them. In another version, given by Rabbi Yehuda, he told them to hurry and do what they needed in the alleyway before nightfall.
why: The mishna mentions a Sadducee where the discussion was about gentiles, and the Gemara explains that a clause is missing: Rabban Gamliel holds that a Sadducee is not like a gentile in these laws. The incident shows him treating the Sadducee's renunciation as valid.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage, who in one version tells of his father's ruling and in another tells his own sons what to do.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage whose version of Rabban Gamliel's words is given first.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who reports Rabban Gamliel's words differently.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group of the Second Temple period that rejected the Sages' oral tradition.
A member of a group similar to the Sadducees that also rejected the Sages' tradition.
Gave up his share in a shared space for Shabbat, so that the other residents may carry there without an eiruv.

note: Rabbi Oshaya's daughter-in-law went to the bathhouse before Shabbat, and it grew dark before she could get back. Her mother-in-law made an eiruv for her so she could return home. The case came before Rabbi Hiyya, who ruled it invalid and forbade her return. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, protested: Babylonian, are you so strict about eiruvin? My father said, wherever you can be lenient with an eiruv, be lenient.
why: Rav holds that a Shabbat-boundary eiruv works only if the food is formally transferred to the person it serves; the Gemara says this is an older dispute and cites the case. Afterward it asks whether Rabbi Hiyya forbade it for lack of transfer or because she did not know of it.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage who ruled the mother-in-law's eiruv invalid.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who objected to Rabbi Hiyya's strictness, quoting his father.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: The father-in-law of the woman stranded at the bathhouse.

terms.meaning: An eiruv of food placed before Shabbat at a spot, letting a person count that spot as home and so walk farther than the usual Shabbat limit.
Rabbi Hiyya had come from Babylonia to the Land of Israel; the address points to his origin.

note: The son of Bonyas came before Rabbi, who told his attendants to make room for a man worth a hundred maneh. Another man came, and Rabbi said to make room for a man worth two hundred maneh. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, told him that the first visitor's father owned a thousand ships at sea and a thousand towns on land. Rabbi replied: when you see his father, tell him not to send his son to me in such clothes.
why: The mishna's example of a landlord's right of usage is the courtyard of the wealthy Bonyas, so the Gemara adds this story about his wealth. Afterward it explains that Rabbi, like Rabbi Akiva, made a point of honoring the rich.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, head of the Sages, who greeted visitors according to their apparent wealth.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who told Rabbi how rich the first visitor's father really was.

people.name: son of Bonyas
people.about: The son of an extremely wealthy man, who came to Rabbi in modest clothes.

terms.meaning: A large unit of money, equal to one hundred zuz. A man worth a hundred maneh was very wealthy.

note: Rav Dimi reported an incident in Tzippori: the people forgot to bring a Torah scroll to the synagogue before Shabbat. The next day, Shabbat, they spread a sheet over the pillars along the way, brought the scroll through the enclosed path and read from it. The Gemara objects that putting up even a temporary tent is forbidden on Shabbat, and corrects the account: they found sheets already spread over the pillars, and used them to bring the scroll and read.
why: The Gemara has argued that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei need not agree about walls that hang down without reaching the ground. The Tzippori incident seemed to rely on such walls, so it says it was done on the authority of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported what happened in Tzippori.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage on whose authority the Tzippori incident was carried out.

terms.meaning: Any makeshift roof or covering. Putting one up counts as building and is forbidden on Shabbat.
From the outset; describing what one may do in the first place, as opposed to what is accepted after the fact.

note: Rabbi recalled that when he and others studied Torah with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa, they would carry oil and a towel from roof to roof, roof to courtyard, courtyard to courtyard, courtyard to enclosure and enclosure to enclosure, until they reached the spring where they bathed. Rabbi Yehuda recalled a time of danger when they carried a Torah scroll from courtyard to roof, roof to courtyard and courtyard to enclosure in order to read from it. The Sages answered him that a time of danger is no proof.
why: The Gemara is weighing how Rav and Rav Yehuda each read the opinions on carrying between roofs, courtyards and enclosures. These memories are a baraita supporting Rav Yehuda's reading that for Rabbi Shimon all of them count as one domain.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who recalled studying with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi's teacher in Tekoa, in whose presence the students carried between roofs, courtyards and enclosures.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who recalled carrying a Torah scroll in a time of danger.

terms.meaning: A fenced area, such as a yard for storage, that is not attached to a house.
A period of persecution when the authorities banned Jewish religious practice.
